projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Theodore E. Sliwa was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II Veteran Theodore E. Silwa. Mr. Silwa served in the U.S. Army with the 552nd Field Artillery Battalion. Ted served in the European Theater, and his highest rank was corporal. I'm Tom Swope, and this recording was made at Mr. Silwa's home in Cleveland, Ohio, on May 9th, 2003. Ted was 81 at the time of this recording. Where were you living in 1941?

sp.speaker: Theodore E. Sliwa
sp.p: I was living in this home in 1941, and in fact, I came here in 1925, to be frank with you, and I have been living here ever since.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Um-hum. How old were you in 1941?

sp.speaker: Theodore E. Sliwa
sp.p: In 1941, I was 20 years old.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So, you were working, I assume?

sp.speaker: Theodore E. Sliwa
sp.p: Yes, I was working. I -- I had just left high school, West Tech, and I got a job at Warner & Swasey on 55th and Carnegie, and at that time, I enjoyed working there very, very much, and the irony of it was that I was there for over a year and a half, and I was making one hundred fifty dollars a week, and then I got a call to the Service, because my Draft Board called then and said, "You're ready to go," and I said, "Well." Then I went down to Ohio State at the time, because I was an Ohio Stater, and then I enlisted in the Army of Ohio State, and then from there I -- I went on to the military, but I must say, from one hundred fifty dollars a week, I went to sixty-five a -- sixty-five -- a hundred and fifty a month -- a hundred and fifty dollars a week to sixty-five dollars a month in the Army.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you have specific memories of December 7th, 1941?

sp.speaker: Theodore E. Sliwa
sp.p: Yes, I do, very specifically. At that time, I was working at Warner & Swasey. It was a Sunday after -- a Sunday evening, and my mother just finished dinner, and we had the radio on, and at that time my mother and dad were there, and my oldest brother Joseph, who was not married, was home at the time, and we were listening to the radio, and all of a sudden, this came over, that we had been invaded in a place called Pearl Harbor, which I didn't know much about Hawaii, but we were told at that time that we were invaded by the Japanese, and that was it. And now this is December 7th. To make a long story short there, my brother -- older brother Joseph was 32 years old, and he had to register for the draft, and what happened to him, he immediately, after the draft started in January, he went in in February, and the irony of the thing was that he went over -- he was a very intelligent person, and -- with the Air Corps and became a astute person with Intelligence, and he went to MacDill Field, Florida at that time and was on a secret mission, so to speak. And he went overseas in '42 with the B-17th, but at that time, with a secret weapon, and that's when he got hurt, and that's the thing I remember about Pearl -- about December 7th. He was the oldest and I was the youngest of seven, and my dad just came home from work at that day, because he worked in the steel mills at Republic Steel. And anyway, I filed that date, and I -- memorably, I'll never forget it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So, when did you go into the Service?

sp.speaker: Theodore E. Sliwa
sp.p: So, what happened, when I went to Ohio State, I immediately -- well, I went into a category of ERC, which is called Enlisted Reserve Corps, and while I was at Ohio State, I was in the School of Administration, and I entered ROTC, Reserve Officers Training Corps, to learn military science for the purpose of the future -- of my intent maybe in the future going into the Service, so I learned military science at Ohio State, and then I partook in military tactics at Ohio State University.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So, then, from Ohio State, you were -- you were drafted out of the --

sp.speaker: Theodore E. Sliwa
sp.p: Well, what happened -- no, I enlisted. I must say that.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You did enlist, okay, all right.

sp.speaker: Theodore E. Sliwa
sp.p: Very, very, very emphatically, I enlisted. They had the Armory, which is a beautiful building in Ohio State -- I wish it was still there -- one of the most beautiful structural businesses or buildings that Ohio State University on the campus, what they call, you know, The Oval. But I got to tell you one thing about Ohio State, I never will forget, very memorably. Every Monday at eleven o'clock, we had Arden Hall. Arden Hall had the bells. The Arden Hall bells began to ring at eleven o'clock, and if you saw the campus at Ohio State, it had various kinds of areas that people can -- they could walk through, the area of the center of campus. They stopped at eleven o'clock on the -- eleven o'clock on a Monday, they had, and the bugle would blow, and everybody would pay honor to the World War I veter -- World War I military people because of -- because the eleventh hour of the eleventh day of the eleventh month was memorable to everybody, and Ohio State always had a commemorating service at that time on Monday, and we stopped at that time. So, after I -- when I was at Ohio State at the time, then I was -- I enlisted. I was foretold -- my sister sent me a notice. She said, "You got your draft notice," and I said, "I don't need it, because I'll leave it to the ERC," and the ERC said, "Yes, you are going to have to go now." This is at Columbus, at Ohio State, and I found out that I was to report to the Induction Center here in Cleveland for active duty on April the 17th of 1943. Well, to speak of it, I was on active -- I was in the military as of November -- November 28th, 1942. I was really on active duty, so to speak, but when I came here, they had to re -- well, they had to re-up me at the Induction Center. They had to take a pledge of -- I didn't have to, but I did -- a pledge of the United States Military, and at that time I -- I went from there, and I went to -- we had to walk over to Terminal Tower, and we were uncertain where we were going to go at the time. I must say I only took my -- my little bag with shaving and personal items in it from the Induction Center, and we walked over to the Terminal Tower, and while I was there waiting for the train to take us to somewhere where I didn't know where, my dad and brother came over, and my dad had tears in his eyes. He came from work, and he saw me off at the Terminal Tower, and I boarded a train -- and boarded a train at that time, and -- [Interview interrupted by a telephone call.]

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: All right, so let's see, where were we? It was April, and you were --

sp.speaker: Theodore E. Sliwa
sp.p: I was at the Terminal Tower, and we were boarding a train, not knowing -- oh, do we want to turn that on again?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah, we were rolling. I turned it on.

sp.speaker: Theodore E. Sliwa
sp.p: All right, we boarded a train not knowing where we would go and went to Camp Perry, here by Lake Erie, which I was surprised to go to, and while there we got our clothing and got our first shots for the military, the tetanus shots and so forth and then typhoid shots, and then -- then they said, "Well, we're going to --" we spent three days there to acclimate ourselves militarily from taps to revelry. I never will forget that. That's very important, it should be to everybody, from -- what I mean by that is five o'clock every day was called retreat. That's when -- whatever you were doing, you stopped, you came into camp, and that's when you had your -- your night dinner. And then after that, you had -- eleven o'clock, you had what they call taps, and everything was quiet. And following that, of course, the next day, you found out what revelry meant, that five o'clock in the morning, they chopped us up a little bit and pull us out of bed at five. I never expected that one, not being used to that kind of living. So, anyhow, we went and spent a few days there, and from there I -- we boarded another train, and we were on this train for -- oh, God, on one day we were there for what -- a day and a half, and we had -- by the way, at nighttime, we had to pull all the curtains down for security reasons, and we went from one town to another, going from Columbus down to -- down to Virginia, from Virginia down to West Virginia, from West Virginia we went from one train to another, and we were now on the train, but we were -- our trains were being sidetracked. We finally end up at Fort Bragg. At that time, it was called -- the town we went into was Pinehurst. That's on the outskirts of Fort Bragg. Fort Bragg is in a little town outside of -- well, it's north of Durham, North Carolina, Fayetteville. That's the base of the -- where the camp is located at Fort Bragg in North Carolina, and I spent 13 weeks in what they call basic training, so I went through that basic training, and while there I was with the -- I was training on field problems with the 82nd Airborne, 503-504 Regiment. These were the initial rangers, so to speak, and I was going to join them to -- because I was in the field problems with them for several weeks. I was supposed to go to Fort Benning, Georgia, but that took place, and finally they read my -- my resume, and they said, "Wait a minute." I wanted to enlist the Airborne -- with Fort Benning to go with the Airborne, and they said, "No, you better not, because we have something else in mind for you," and I said, "What was that?" "Well," they said, "because you had military science, you had an administrative background from Ohio State, you also have a language, we're sending you to Citadel University in Charleston, South Carolina, and there you're going to be with ASTP, Army Specialized Training, which led into what they call Intelligence, G-2. So, I spent a month there, and after that, I was informed that I was going to go to Fort Sill, Oklahoma to get my commission, but they said, "No, we're sending you back to Fort Bragg." I says, "Well, why Fort Bragg again?" "Well, we need you for cadre." So, I went back to Fort Bragg, and I became cadre, that's another 13-week cycle, and I said, "After that, I'll be going to Fort Sill, Oklahoma?" They said, "Oh, no." So, after 13 weeks, I found out that we went through the infiltration courses. Infiltration courses are things when they fire three feet above you day and night, you had to go through that course with live ammunition being -- and barbed wire above you for three feet, and also they put us through a very strange training called gas mask training. At that time, because the Germans had gas masks, gas training -- gas in World War I, they had put us through gas mask training. I went through that for about a week, which was a -- it was a nasty thing. You had to go into various kinds of buildings with gas, came out coughing and so forth, but then they gave you a gas mask, weighed 16 pounds. So, you had to go in with a gas mask. So, I went through that training thinking when we hit Europe, we were going wherever it was they had to have gas masks. So, I carried that gas mask after that, and -- 16 pounds of it, and I thought after the 13-week cycle, I was going to go back to Fort Sill -- go to Fort Sill, Oklahoma, and they said, "Well, no," they said, "We got you alerted." I says, "For what?" They says, "Well, you're going for the European Theater." I said, "Oh, my gosh," because I had some intelligence background, and I was a forward observer, so to speak, at the time they made me a forward observer at Fort Bragg, and I -- when I was taking my cadre training, which meant I could fire artillery pieces or mortars for that matter. They put you up in front in the Infantry sometimes so you could support them with either mortars or artillery or whatever kind of weapon you needed for support.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How would you communicate back to the artillery?

sp.speaker: Theodore E. Sliwa
sp.p: Beg your pardon?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How would you communicate back to the artillery?

sp.speaker: Theodore E. Sliwa
sp.p: Oh, by -- by telephone. We used to --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Telephone lines?

sp.speaker: Theodore E. Sliwa
sp.p: The telephone lines, usually telephone lines, and we -- we would go -- be ahead of the battalion, so to speak, and then they'd give us what they call a -- maps with grids on them. Grids were -- were 100 yard squares, and they showed you the terrain, and they showed you on these -- you had to carry that big thing around you, it was cumbersome, the thing is about two feet square, in a leather bag -- in a leather compartment. So, we were told that when I went to -- overseas, I -- I went on a troop ship called the AQUITANIA. The AQUITANIA is a ship that had 10,000 American troops on it, and at that time, the German submarines were very heavy in the North -- North Atlantic, and the thing that surprised me, we had 10,000. I slept about two tiers above four -- we had tiers of four in our compartments of sleeping in the lower part of the ship, and we went across, and I noticed that we were unescorted. The last I ever saw was a PBY Navy plane out of Halifax, Canada, and we were going -- heading for the Atlantic unescorted. And then I noticed, this was a ship that had 30 knots on it, could go 30 knots. It made us go zig-zag. That's all we were doing on the North Atlantic was zig-zagging and hitting a few storms. After ten days, we hit Scotland, called -- called -- not far from Edinboro, we hit Scotland, and we deboarded and went to the train station, and from there we were alerted. I'll never forget Scotland, because I love -- one thing about the British Army, they have a sergeant major, and he was a big guy usually, and this guy was a big one, and he always had a stick -- he always used to carry a stick, but he was spic and span, and he had -- his trousers were pressed properly, and whatever he said, I couldn't understand half of the time. So, they took 500 of us and put us on that train station platform, and the officers were not allowed to talk to anybody, so he took command, and he says, "Oh, yeah, oh, whatever happened to that --" we just kept on going. Anyway, we left Scotland, and being with the training I went through, we had to go through a town called Cardiff, Wales, what they call artillery training, where we fired our weapons then at that time at Cardiff, Wales, and it was a small community, but Cardiff is the capital of Wales, but it was a small community. The Welsh people -- well, the Scotch people were very good and the Scotch people were very nice to us and the Welsh people were very nice. Then we went down to Britain, or down to England, and then we hit a town called Weymouth. That's on the -- not far from Southampton. It's on the port side of England, and we were preparing. We were taking basic training on boarding and deboarding a ship with the big guidelines with which you -- with your full pack. So, we trained there for a while. Then we got the alert, and we found out that the alert came in for -- we didn't know the invasion, and we saw airplanes going and we saw -- oh, by the way, that's -- when I hit Scotland, that was the first time -- well, anyway, when I got aboard ship state-side, the first thing I learned about blackout. No lighting during the daytime. That's -- I spent 11 months of that, just blackouts. So, after --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: When did you arrive in Scotland?

sp.speaker: Theodore E. Sliwa
sp.p: Beg your pardon?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: When did you arrive in Scotland? When did you --

sp.speaker: Theodore E. Sliwa
sp.p: I arrived in -- in March, I think the date was the 23rd, of '44.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: 1944, okay.

sp.speaker: Theodore E. Sliwa
sp.p: And then hit the -- we were boarding ships, and then we boarded an LST, landing ship transport, because we had a lot of equipment, military -- artillery pieces and mostly shells and -- and quartermaster, we had to have -- well, everybody has to have a quartermaster. A quartermaster is the one who feeds you and houses you when you go into combat. So, we -- we were there, and we were being bombed day and night by the Germans. We were, by the -- the German fighter planes, the Messerschmidts. The Messerschmidt was a big, beautiful plane, but it was a nasty thing that used to fire a lot, and they also used it -- they had a thing called the VE bomb, the Germans had --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: VE bomb, right.

sp.speaker: Theodore E. Sliwa
sp.p: -- which we never heard about before, and this thing was unmanned, and they used to fire it from Germany, fire into various towns of England, like Coventry. They killed several hundred thousand people with those. And once in a while, the irony was these VE things would turn around and go back to Germany and blow up somewhere. But we went through that counter-fire with that, and then the -- once in a while we would learn about the Germans being with their ships, coming along and bombing Weymouth or Southampton, and we got the alert on the -- I think it was on the 1st of June and anticipating to go any time after that. So, they hit the beach on June 6th of 1944, and I went with a -- we were assigned to a ship which housed the -- what they called the Fourth Infantry Division, and we hit a town outside of -- called Omaha in the English Channel outside of Normandy. Utah was the -- was the -- I'm sorry, I beg off on that one. The town that was hit first was Omaha.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Omaha.

sp.speaker: Theodore E. Sliwa
sp.p: That's where the American Service took a very serious beating, hitting that, because then we hit a -- we hit the port called Utah, Utah in Normandy. But to make a long story short about Omaha, Hitler decided -- Rommel made all the things to defend. Omaha -- Falaise Gap, Falaise Gap is the shortest distance between England and France, but they put various kinds of weaponry to anticipate our invasion there, and Rommel set this whole thing up was -- he had various things, like tie tracks, and he had the bomb -- I mean, he had detonating bombs and so forth that would detonate at times. And the other part that Germany did, they had -- all their Panzer Divisions were outside of Pas-de-Calais. Hitler thought they were going to hit at Pas-de-Calais, which is the shortest distance between England and France, and luckily, they weren't there, because we would have had a tough time, much tougher than we had at Omaha. We hit Utah, and then after Utah, why I --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you land on Utah Beach, then?

sp.speaker: Theodore E. Sliwa
sp.p: Utah Beach.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: On -- was -- did you land on June 6th?

sp.speaker: Theodore E. Sliwa
sp.p: June -- no, no, June 8th.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You landed -- okay.

sp.speaker: Theodore E. Sliwa
sp.p: Several days later, and then I hit -- by the way, I carried that gas mask. That gas mask was mandatory to carry with -- and besides a Mae West. Mae West was a big thing you put over your waist in case you get hit on the sea, you can float, and I carried that and my -- my battle pack, and we hit Utah, and somehow they sent us up to a town called La Hai Dupree (ph), which is the northern tip of Normandy where the 101st Airborne was there, and they were taking a heavy casualty rate, but they needed our support. So, we went up there, and it's the first time I ever observed any combat, is at La Hai Dupree (ph) in northern Normandy. And we survived that somehow, and the thing that -- the irony that helped -- that I hit the beach at Utah, I saw one of the first American casualties, which was a youngster. I don't think he even shaved. He was very -- it depressed me greatly to see this youngster, he was killed, and he was laying alongside the road, and -- by the way, in Normandy, we hit Normandy, you had to watch out for -- they had a thing called octomienen (ph), the Germans, German, octomienen, land mines. So, you had to watch where you walked. You had to watch -- you had to make sure -- I'd usually follow the trail of a car or a truck, because then you knew they went over it, there weren't any land mines left, so to speak, but the trouble with those land mines, sometimes you could -- we had detonators that could check where the land mines were, but the Germans were smart. They used plastic, where you couldn't -- you couldn't check the detonations, and then that's when our force -- when I hit, up there at La Hai Dupree (ph), I saw American Airborne men which I regretted -- regrettably saw several hanging in the trees up in that area. So, from there, then we went over to ourselves and finally conquered that area, and we went down south to Calais -- not Calais, but it was a town outside of -- south -- oh yeah, Saint-Lo. What happened in Normandy, there was an arc. If you could look at the map of Normandy, you'll see it all the way from Omaha Beach over to the corner of -- see, Normandy is a peninsula, and it's like an arc, and you go from there -- and we were coming down, we had trouble, and we couldn't penetrate this arc. For some reason, the Germans brought their Panzers up, and they -- they held us longly -- longer than we thought it would be in a town called Saint-Lo. Saint-Lo was a pivotal town. It had roads and railroads and everything going into it. It's a pivotal town right in the center of the arc of Normandy, and of all things, I hadn't seen General Herr or General Patton, but I heard he was in England, and somehow they brought him in. They were stuck, and Eisenhower and Brodie got together and said, "Gee, we've got to get George up here," being George Patton, Junior, the greatest military commander I ever saw, heard about and followed. They brought him through, and somehow he set up his -- his tanks, and the irony of the thing was that he studied the book of Rommel. Rommel was a great tank general. Von Guderian was the -- was the guy that made the Panzer Division -- the Panzer tank was a beautiful tank, very -- very high fire power, and somehow Pat -- Patton studied Rommel, and he somehow broke through at Saint-Lo. And the Army at that time, Rommel had to go home on sick leave or something, he wasn't there at the time of the break-through at Saint-Lo. That was about July 16th or so of '44, and Patton broke through, and he went through like you wouldn't believe with his tanks. He knew how to maneuver them and everything, thank God for Patton, and so we -- from there we went on, and then we went into -- we got through France, and I ended up in a town called Kakarata, Holland.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Were you with the Fourth Infantry at this time?

sp.speaker: Theodore E. Sliwa
sp.p: No, I'm not. No, being with the artillery, you're -- you're under the command of what they call Artillery Support. Usually you're assigned by the Corps, and at that time, we were assigned to the Seventh Corps, and they would send us wherever we needed fire power, and at that time, we divert. From there we went -- we supported the Second Armored Division, like I said, up in Normandy, we supported the 101st Airborne Division, and then we supported -- down here in Saint-Lo, we supported the Second Armored Division, we supported the First Infantry Division, we supported the -- the -- as I recall, the -- others that were there that -- speaking of, , I was trying to remember the insignia that some of these -- of these divisions. And we supported many divisions at that time, because of the fire power support, and after that, we left the town of Kakarata, and I became a -- being an FO -- being a forward observer, called FOP, I went to a town called Kakarata, and the first time I ever had observed from a church steeple. Of all things, I had to go at night -- I had to go to work in the morning at two o'clock in the morning, because we had to go sometimes ahead of the Infantry to check our -- we also had radios, but we had what they called a BC scope. They use them now I understand in Iraq. A BC scope is a scope that has crossroads on it, but it illuminates at night, and at that time, you have to see where you're firing, what directions and so forth, because the artillery, one thing people don't know about artillery, you just can't start firing wherever you want to, because you will be firing on your own personnel. And then from there, we went to Kakarata, and we got through there. Kakarata mostly is a mining town of Holland. We went to a town called -- in Belgium, then I hit Belgium, and at that time we hit -- somehow the troops came in and liberated Paris, which I was -- we should have been there, but we were far ahead of them, so we weren't in the march, and in Paris, the troops that were there were the 28th Division. These people didn't see any combat even for that matter, many of them didn't. But anyway, thank God we liberated Paris, and from there we went on to Belgium, and then from Belgium we went back south, and we had a problem at a town called -- outside of the Rhine River called Remagen, and we couldn't cross the Rhine for some reason. The Germans were holding it tight. They were really -- we were in a combat situation all along the Rhine. We should have been in -- across the Rhine in November of '44, but somehow Eisenhower got the cute idea, which I don't understand where he got it from, the British, General Montgomery, to go up to a town called Nijmegen in Holland, and Nijmegen was a pivotal town up in Holland there, because it has roads and it had various kinds of approaches for entry into Holland by rail or by roads. And what I regret at that time is, like I said, it was November of -- September of '44, we were going due east, going towards the Rhine River to get -- we thought we were going to Berlin by Christmas of 1944, but at that time, Ike gave the order to ration, which meant in the artillery, we had ten shells a day, and they even stopped giving gas to Patton. Patton was stopped even giving gas. The men had to stop cold, because they had no gas, and they diverted this equipment to the north, to Nijmegen, and they alerted the American 82nd, the American 101st, the British Second Devil Brigade and the Polish Brigade, which was airborne, to drop on Nijmegen. And that's what -- was Montgomery's idea, but Patton was talked into it -- Eisenhower was talked into it, and when they dropped, they made a very serious mistake up there militarily. They didn't check it out close enough. They finally captured Nijmegen, but we lost several -- 11,000 men there because the Germans were smart. They had a Panzer Division facing them, and what the irony was, they should never have dropped in the daytime. They dropped in the daytime, and there was a -- there was a holy mess up there militarily, and we lost a lot of manpower up there.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That would be Operation Market-Garden, right?

sp.speaker: Theodore E. Sliwa
sp.p: That's right, Mark -- that's right, Mark -- that's the phrase they used for it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Now, before we get to the Bulge, do you have any other vivid memories of the campaign in Normandy?

sp.speaker: Theodore E. Sliwa
sp.p: The thing that I remember of Normandy basically is the hedge rows, those are nasty things. See, instead of having fences and sort of build things, the French farmers usually built hedge rows. What they did is they -- on their borderline, they put a lot of -- a lot of land and bricks, rocks and interweaving vines of all kind, and they called it the hedge row district. I never forgot that, and because every time we would go somewhere, the Germans would come from behind the hedge rows and they were firing at us from all directions, and the hedge rows were a nasty thing. We had to use tanks, which they had front-end loaders to break through those hedge rows, because the Germans were counter-attacking through those hedge rows. They were hiding behind the hedge rows. And also I remember about Normandy is that -- it's a beautiful area for -- for orchards, apple orchards and so forth, and that's where I first got my first taste of -- of -- the Americans, they use apple cider, but that's where I first tasted cider, and -- not first tasted it, but that's where the French had -- that was very common up there, and the farmers were nice to us. That's the one thing I remember about Normandy, also, is the farmers had -- they worked in the fields. They didn't know what time of day it was. They didn't have no watches. So, they used to listen to the bells in the steeple, the church, and they used to have chapels on the outskirts of the churches, and you could see the farmers or the -- even the nuns, for that matter, come out and pray, right in these little chapels along the roads in Normandy, and -- oh, yes, I must say one more thing about Normandy. It rained quite a bit, and we had rain showers quite a bit, and it was dusty after that, it would dry for a while, and I remember the French -- the French -- oh, yeah, we came into a -- Normandy, we came into a thing called the French FFI. They had a band on the left hand, they called them Freedom Fighters of Interior of France. They wore bands with white -- with the -- with the Alsace Cross on it with the FFI on it, and they came across. They were our undercover men, and they were all civilians, but -- well, maybe they were military, but they were dressed in civilian clothes with those bands, and they helped us to -- giving us instructions about the Germans. They used to spy on the Germans for us, and I remember that, too. And I remember the French farmers that were very humble people, very, very nice to us, whichever was left. We saw many dead cows, and I never forgot that, because most of the cows that we saw were bloated already. They were all killed and laying in the fields, and they had beautiful agriculture there in that sector. And after we left there, I couldn't remember the -- some of the people that helped us go through that warfare there, and -- oh, yeah, one more thing I remember about Normandy, which I do think the Americans don't give or the military give enough credit to are the Gurkha Indians, G R U H K A (sic), Indians. They usually wore turbans, and we used to see them once in a while in Normandy, and they always carried round knives. They never spoke much English, but there were -- they were directed by the British who spoke their language, and we couldn't talk to them, because they wouldn't talk to us, because you couldn't understand them. But the irony of them, when they would go into an area where the enemy was, we usually saw the decapitated soldiers always, because they couldn't talk to them. They wouldn't talk to anybody, and they just waylaid anybody who was in front of them, but they don't -- I don't know, I think Eisenhower should give more credit to them, because they were excellent. And by the way, they come from Nepal and not from India. I think that should be remembered. And they should give more credit to those people. And we had freedom fighters from Poland, France -- Poland and -- and other areas, some other nationality were there, but I noticed the Polish because I spoke the language and Slavish, Czechs. Anyway, Normandy, we got through that all right, and like I said, we hit outside of -- outside of the Rhine and they directed everybody to Nijmegen. That was a mistake militarily, because we could have gone across the Rhine. We could have been in Berlin by -- by Christmas of 1944, because we had the whole German situation -- if they had these troops up north, then maybe we could have gone south and gone through without much opposition, because they didn't have the reserve power. The reserve power was up north in Nijmegen, and of course, they -- I think we lost that battle in a way, but militarily, we got -- we recovered to Nijmegen. After that, we got along the Rhine, and we finally got back to normal in October of '44, and by that I mean they started giving us ammunition on -- giving us petroleum or they call it petrol. The thing that I've got to remember about that, about the Rhine, is that they had -- they called it the Red Ball Express, because at that time all of the trains and all the roads were bombed, so they had to use the -- the Americans had the -- the American quartermaster shot up a truck thing called the Red Ball Express, and they lined them up. They were all Diamond Ts full of equipment and ammunition and all kinds of medical supplies and everything, but they called it the Red Ball Express, and they brought in our equipment that we needed as we were going along because we needed -- well, you have to have food supplies, you have to have military -- or medical supplies, you have to have military supplies. They brought them through in those trucks, but it -- I don't think -- I think it should be mentioned about the Red Ball Express. It was a savior for us transportation-wise. And then we got down along the Rhine and we got stuck at the Rhine, because the Germans were very heavily fortified across the Rhine River, and I -- I was assigned to the Ninth Armored Division at the time for Remagen, R E I M G E N (sic), and Remagen was a small town with a bridge. Now, you see, across the Rhine, they have these bridges. Most of them at that time were blown up, and ironically, this one bridge at Remagen was not blown up, and the German colonel was supposed to blow it up or had it detonated -- by the way, they had detonation to blow it up, but somehow we got down there, and I got -- I was a forward observer, and we were furrowing over this bridge, and then all of a sudden there was Ninth Armored Division Infantry, a Polish kid from Toledo, who was squad sergeant, and they told him not to go on the bridge, it was detonated, but he went across with his squad. And he made a -- he got a hold across the bridge, he got a foothold militarily across the bridge, and they just started all coming over. You couldn't take tanks or nothing, because it would detonate them -- I mean, it would detonate the bridge, but they had enough manpower across the bridge to make a hold across the Rhine. That was the first time we ever got across the Rhine. And in the meantime, Patton to the south was using pontoon bridges, which we did after that. We had them, too, in the first time, but the third time we had it, and then we had the pontoon bridges on the south. He got across on pontoon bridges, but what I might say is, Remagen bridge after we got across, they probably blew it up, and thank God for the smartness of the Ninth Armored Infantry, and we got a foothold across the Rhine River. Then we went on from that, and then all of a sudden -- oh, yeah, before I forget --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Remagen was after the Battle of the Bulge, wasn't it?

sp.speaker: Theodore E. Sliwa
sp.p: Yes, yes. I better get back to my --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Let's get back to the Battle of the Bulge, and then we can come back to it.

sp.speaker: Theodore E. Sliwa
sp.p: Let me get back to it. I'm sorry about that.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That's all right.

sp.speaker: Theodore E. Sliwa
sp.p: I go back to the point that we got into a -- into Belgium, and we had a problem at the time. This was the winter of 1944, and the temperatures were hitting around 15 to 20 degrees below zero, and we were called to support units up in a town called -- the main town was Bastogne, but the town we had to go to was Hiafelise (ph) and St. Vith, which are on the outskirts of Bastogne, and we supported that, but then we were told militarily -- in fact, I understand Patton told Eisenhower that the Germans were concentrating their armored divisions east of Bastogne, and -- well, Eisenhower didn't take that seriously, because he felt that this terrain was -- it's spa country. It's beautiful hilly country, farm country mostly, forests, pine forests and so forth and hilly, but they were all frozen, and Eisenhower didn't think or First Army Generals Bradley and Eisenhower didn't think they were going to come through there and anything. But they had Germans on the 16th of December -- this was before the 16th of December, they brought up a division called the 106th Lionhead Division, which had 18,000 men, and this was about -- around the early part of December of '44. And they brought in 18,000 men, but these were young -- just young troops, just came from the States. They were only in basic training, 13-18 weeks, and they were still like ODs and so forth, and why they put them in that position, but the reason was militarily is to give them R&R, rehabilitation and retrain, in case they checked them. They didn't think there could be much combat going on over there, and -- so, it was a loose area, so to speak. Militarily, it wasn't very heavily defended. And then the Germans made a thrust -- this was where Hitler made a decision to thrust outside the Bulge and outside of Bastogne, and he thrust forward on the 16th of December. And at that time, the 106th was in front with 18,000 men. On the 18th of December, they only had 8002 men left. 10,000 were either killed or froze to death in that one battle, the Battle of the Bulge. And we were trying to concentrate on a town called Hiafelise (ph) and St. Vith, and we tried to penetrate their outer circles, but somehow Bastogne was the key. If you take -- look at it like a U shape, it's in the middle of the U, and we had a lot of trouble in that area because of the weather and the German's heavy Panzer Divisions were catching our toll where casualties were very high. And one of the things that they should have taught the American Servicemen, which they didn't, which I learned as a youngster, keep your clothes dry but change your socks every day, and most of the Servicemen did not change their socks in the Battle of the Bulge, and they caught a thing called trench foot. What that is is when a trooper would take off his shoes, simply if he didn't change his clothes in that cold weather or his socks within two-three -- for three days basically, he took skin with it. They call it trench foot. We had many casualties with that, and I changed socks every day, because they asked me how many socks I wanted, and I said I wanted 16 pairs, because I'm not going to -- I'm not going to wash socks, which we usually did, in cold weather, and so I had to change them every day, threw my old socks away. And at Bastogne, we were stuck, and all of a sudden, Eisenhower was -- was in a real mess here militarily. In fact, he fired Bradley. Bradley was in charge of the group which had the Third and the American First Army and the British Second Army -- no, the British Army -- Second Army was under General Montgomery. The First Army was under General Bradley, with the First Army and the Ninth Army were under his command, and to the south was Patton, who was with the Third Army, but Bradley was fired as the group commander of that. That's where he should have -- I think he made a big mistake, because he didn't realize what he did militarily wrong. And I understand from about the 24th, Eisenhower called Patton up. He said, "I need you up here," and Patton was going towards Metz and going due east into Germany, going towards Berlin -- not Berlin, but across towards the Rhine, I'm sorry, the Rhine, and he says -- and Patton had 340,000 men facing due east in cold weather, 15 degrees below zero. Ike says, "George, I need you up here badly north of Bastogne." He said, "Ike, I did it two days ago." He diverted 340,000 men from due east to due north, and at that time, when we had -- just before we hit Bastogne, the German commander went up to a talented, tough Irish commander called General Anthony McAuliffe (ph) of the 101st Airborne, and this Irishman was from Boston, a tough fist-fighting one, got to give a lot of credit, because he analyzed -- the German officer came in with the white flag, and he came up to his headquarters, and he said to his interpreter, in English, "You tell him to surrender or we're going to annihilate you." He goes, "What's that?" He said, "We're going to annihilate you if you don't surrender." And he thought in his little maddish -- in his Irish way, he says, "Nuts." Out of nowhere, he said, "Nuts." When the word came back to the German commander from this interpreter, he says, [German], "What's going on up there? What did he say to you?" He says, "Nuts." And he said [German], he got angry, angry like he was going to blow up. Well, somehow in the meantime when Patton came due north, he somehow penetrated that arc of the Bulge, and he came up to Bastogne where the commander was, General Anthony McAuliffe, the commander of the 101st Airborne. He looked at him and he says, "You know, I have to tell you something. You have the most beautiful speech that I ever heard in my life, excellent speech," he said. And anyway, commanded him from that and so forth. They saved -- Bastogne was saved by the 101st Airborne, and Patton came through with his Third Army, and see, Patton should have got credit for that, but it seemed every time Patton won a battle, Ike got a star or someone. I don't know what it was all about, that European Theater. And then finally we got through that, and we got to the Rhine and got through to Remagen and got through like I told you before.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Where were you exactly when the Bulge broke?

sp.speaker: Theodore E. Sliwa
sp.p: I was at a town called Hiafelise (ph), Bulligan.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Was your town overrun?

sp.speaker: Theodore E. Sliwa
sp.p: Beg pardon?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Was your town overrun by the Germans?

sp.speaker: Theodore E. Sliwa
sp.p: Oh, no, it wasn't. I was on the outskirts. There's not many towns up there. Bulligan is a little town where we put our artillery pieces, and outside of Hiafelise (ph), which is -- it's west of Bastogne. We were -- we were surviving there pretty good, because we got our -- somehow we got our fire power up because of the -- END OF SIDE ONE, TAPE ONE; BEGIN SIDE TWO, TAPE ONE.

sp.speaker: Theodore E. Sliwa
sp.p: -- what happened was that when Patton was told he was going to go up there, he went to his chaplain. He was the only one that had a Catholic chaplain, by the name of O'Neil, (ph) Colonel O'Neil (ph). He went up to him and he says, "Colonel," he says, "I need a -- I need a prayer." He said, "I've got to get a prayer here to -- to tell the Lord to skip -- clear the sky so I can kill those Huns." He's like, "I can't do that." He says, "That's -- that's against my religion to talk like that." He says, "I want a prayer." He made a prayer. I have a -- I don't have it here in front of me, but he made a prayer up about -- asking the Lord to open the skies for better weather, and that's all he -- I don't know how he said it, but he did say it, and somehow, after about the 24th when Patton -- or 25th -- came up, the skies were open. That's when the Air Corps came out. Finally we got support from the Air Corps, which we needed badly. At that time, the German Air Corps was defunct, so to speak. They weren't active as much, but they were around from time to time, but there weren't that many left, and the Air Corps was superior, and they helped us -- they went behind the German lines and they bombed their support units and everything that were coming up militarily with their manpower or equipment, and they bombed all the bridges, and they didn't have any kind of support, so the prayer helped and the good Lord helped and we broke through, and thanks to Patton and all of the military tactics.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Tell me about the goose.

sp.speaker: Theodore E. Sliwa
sp.p: Well, anyway, just before we left my area outside of Bulligan, I was in a castle, called the Castle of the Cold Heart. The name of the town slips me right now, but as a -- it's right outside of -- a beautiful area out there outside of Spa in Holland or Belgium, and I was out on a maneuver -- on a field problem, I had to go check something in the woods or something, and I -- I noticed something following me. It was a goose, and this goose happened to have a feather that was a -- he had been probably hit by shrapnel or something, but he only had half a wing, and he was following me all over, and I finally got the -- I called him Zoo-Zoo for some reason. I -- I found him, and I found something -- gave him something to eat all the time. He followed me all over the place, and I finally took him in as a little pet, and I called him Zoo-Zoo, and I told my friends in the military, I says, "Don't you ever touch my goose," because they wanted to eat him, the goose. I said, "You're going to get something to reckon with me. We are going to have an altercation here." Anyway, just before I left that Castle of the Cold Heart, we had to observe from the -- they had a fire watch near that house. See, the hills of Belgium had fire watches, which were made of wood, and you could observe for fires, but we observed it for forward observers, and then just before I left, I gave it to -- I saw a farmer. I says, "Take care of my goose." He looked at the goose, and he says, "Yeah, I'll take care of my goose." I said, "He's a good one, call him Zoo-Zoo or something," and I left him there, and I went on to -- to my campaigning. I had to go forward with my jeep, and I went forward after that, and forward we went, and went through that German area after Remagen, and we were going -- heck bent for -- for Berlin, and on my jeep, I had, "On to Berlin," and somehow when I got -- we got closer, I got to a town called Magdaberg, and I'll never forgot it, because outside of Magdaberg, they had a whole -- I never saw this before, but I must go back. One thing in November of 1944, first time I ever saw a airplane which was not fueled, but the airplanes at that time were considered what we have now, jets. I saw two German jets, and what I mean by that, they were flying high, and our P-47s or P-51s couldn't catch them. They were fast. They were way above. It's the first time I ever heard of a German jet. It was in November of 1944, and the Germans had them. And outside of a town called Magdaberg, I came into this town and we found a whole hillside, it's on the outskirts of a little country town, it had all kinds of jet engines burned. The Germans burned them. That's where I saw my first jet engines, and they were 90 miles from Berlin, and we were going to go to Berlin within about a week. In five days we would be in Berlin, but all of a sudden, Patton was to my south with the Third Army, and he was at a town called Prague, Czechoslovakia. He was more than miles away from Berlin. We were 90 miles away. Then we got an order, which I never could understand why we got that order, is you will stop where you're at. I says, "For God's sakes, not now, let's get to Berlin." And it came down to me through certain quarters that Eisenhower made a deal with the Russians, and he didn't even contact Churchill from what I understand, gave it to the Russians, and I couldn't believe we were stopped there, and I wanted to go into Berlin, what we thought should have been ours, which could have been, but somehow the politics came into the picture, and that's one thing Patton told Eisenhower. He said, "You know one thing, I'm not a politician, I'm a military man," and we didn't -- we didn't get to Berlin. Then they asked -- not far from Berlin to the west, it was called Elbe River, E L B E River, and that's where the Russians came in, and that's when we were told to stop. But then they asked me if I wanted to go up to shake hands with the Russians. I says, "Look, Mack, no way would I shake hands with the Russians." I agree with Patton, they are a common enemy, but at that time, you know, militarily they're our friends, but I didn't go up to shake hands with them at the Elbe River, and -- but after that, they -- the war ended in May 4th of 1945, and I was in this town Magdaberg. Then I went to a town called Stolberg. That's sort of a big, beautiful town in Germany, and that's where I have some of my equipment I got. I got some beautiful things from there that they gave me, and -- not equipment, but souvenirs and so forth. And then I was told to go to Leon, France, and at that time they were considering me to go -- they said, "Well, we have you earmarked for an officership," which I should have gotten before we went overseas, but they said, "We've got you earmarked for officership to go to the east, go to Japan, go towards the Pacific." And that meant that I had to go from Leon, which is the middle part of France, you go south to Marseilles. Marseilles is where they were shipping you all out. You had to go through the Suez Canal to get to the Pacific, and my -- my situation was, one, that I -- after five battles, I've seen enough. I think my time was up, and my number was up, too, because I was close many, many times of meeting the -- the ones that never came back. And I said to the commander, I says, "You've had me alerted for this." I said, "By the way, this point system --" and he says, "Yes," he says, "You've got quite a few because you've got five per battle, five points per battle," and he said, "By the way, how many do you need to -- to go State-side?" "72." "How many do I have?" "80 -- 84," I think it was he said. I says, "Commander, good-bye." So, I took my leave there, and I said, "I'm leaving. I am going to go State-side." I don't know if it's going to be -- because the war in Japan wasn't over yet. This is May I'm talking about; I'm not talking about -- this was going into -- well, August was the date of the Japanese surrender. Yes, I was supposed to go there in July, and then I hit Le Havre in France, they traveled me on -- I took my jeep up to Le Havre in France, and that's where I boarded a ship to go to the States on a Liberty ship with 8000 of us, boy, bouncing around on the ocean like a -- like a ball of some kind, up and down. But we finally got to home after ten days on the ocean, I got to New York or to Boston, rather, to Boston Harbor. Then from Boston Harbor, they said, "Well, we're sending you to Harrisburg to alert you if you have to go anywhere." I says, "Look, how many points do I have, hey, Bubba?" So, I got 84 points. They said, "We're sending you to Indiantown Gap, Harrisburg, Pennsylvania." I said, "Well, good." Well, I got there, and he says, "Well, you made it, Mack, you made it. You're being told that your service days are over." That's where I was discharged, at Harrisburg, Pennsylvania, and I came home -- this was November of 1945. I remember coming home out of Pennsylvania Station, I had to take a bus from the -- the Pennsylvania Station was where the old stadium used to be, there was a Pennsylvania Station there, take a bus to get home, and I came home and didn't tell my mother, because I didn't want to call her and surprise her or shock her, because my brother at that time was racked up pretty badly. He was in a hospital State-side. I came home, and I -- I hit the front sidewalk right by the steps, where they are now, I kissed it. I finally made it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you lose any close buddies over there?

sp.speaker: Theodore E. Sliwa
sp.p: Many, I lost many of them, yes. I hate to go into that, but there are some that I can't forget about, because they were so close to me at times. One was a fellow from California that was right close to me, and he took military basic training with me at Fort Bragg, and then he went through the Service with me, and he got -- he got hit with a German shell. Germans had a piece of equipment that was -- that we Americans are beginning to use very heavily called an 88. An 88 at that time was the German artillery piece but used for anti-aircraft and for firing power, but the thing that made you psychologically go -- get nervous was a thing called a Screaming Mimi, and this 88 had -- if you look at the end of a barrel, like on the end of our artillery barrel, you'll see there are openings. There are openings in the end of the barrel, which we never had before, and somehow this artillery piece that they shot was a Screaming Mimi. This thing helped it, when it went through the air, it started screaming, real screaming. You'd think it was going to hit you. It would cover the whole area. One shell would cover the whole area. You'd be in a fox where you think it's going to fall right in on you, but the Screaming Mimi was a nasty military psychological thing, because many fellows went nuts, because as soon as they saw that, they jumped out of their foxholes, which they shouldn't have, they thought they were going to get hit, because it was so -- it was a piece that I never will forget called a Screaming Mimi. And then I -- I wanted to go back to one more thing about the military. I will say this for them, that whoever handled their -- their catering was very good, because they had a thing called K-rations. K-rations was cans, and it usually had some kind of scrambled eggs in it, in the can, and Spam, I remember Spam very well, and dry crackers. And we had a C-ration, which was in a can -- your food was in a can with a cracker, cracker, was what I call it on top, and the bottom it had the food, you could warm it up, you could heat it and you could eat it. Then the worst -- the third one that I never will forget was called a D-bar. A D-bar was a little square thing about a half inch by two inches long. It was encased in -- in an encasement, and it was very heavily encased, and when you opened the thing, you had a D-bar, and then the D-bar was supposed to have a food value for a whole day, one D-bar, and it was encased very heavily, and it was a small piece, like I said, about a half inch wide and about two inches long and about an inch and a half wide, but I mean, I'm trying to get the length -- the length is about two inches, and the width is about an inch and a half. And you opened it up, and then you -- what I did, smartly, which many men didn't do was I -- my mother taught me, you are what you eat. So, I notched it with my bayonet, I'd notch it for breakfast, lunch and dinner, on the D-bar. So, I just took what I needed for the breakfast, lunch and dinner. My other fellow mates did not do that. They would eat the whole thing in the morning, and then they were looking for grass and everything they could eat, berries or anything. But luckily, I survived with a D-bar, which I -- one day at Fort Bragg, before we left the States, by the way, they put us in the field. They said, "We are going to give you just strictly a D-bar." That's all we had for the whole day, is a D-bar. So, I had to -- I put my three -- two notches in it, and I had lunch -- breakfast, lunch and dinner. Some of my friends were eating dandelions and they're eating all kinds of grass and all kind of weeds they could get. Anyhow, those are the things that you recall, as I do at this time, because many years have passed, and things have begun to fade away, so to speak. And I must say one more thing in conclusion here. I believed in two terminologies that General MacArthur, General of the Army, Douglas MacArthur said, which are very, very valiant and prevalent, should be prevalent. The first was, "Duty, honor, country." And the second one I'll never forget, which we haven't done, "War's ultimate aim is victory, not indecisive indecision." Those remarks would be wholesome today, which they should be, and haven't been. We haven't done that in Korea, we haven't done it in Vietnam, and I hope we do it in Iraq. I hope we do our duty, but I still can't understand the military technique of the Americans today. We're so diversified militarily over the world, because I'm most interested in security of the United States, and to this day, I can't understand why we need security, why are we maintaining 37,000 troops in Korea. I'm thinking of our security in this country. Why do we have 15,000 in Yugoslavia? Why are we securing everybody else, when we have to protect our own shores? We do it now with security people, but we're using our American -- we're depleting our defensive forces here, but I'm an American first, and I believe in that, that's my opinion, which I'm entitled to, and I think we should take care of this country. It's the greatest country in the world, and God bless it. God bless America. That's all I can tell you.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: When you think about that experience overseas, does any other particularly vivid memory come to mind?

sp.speaker: Theodore E. Sliwa
sp.p: The one thing I remember going over on the ship, the AQUITANIA, which had 10,000 of us, I was with the -- the deck, I was on a Bofor gun. A Bofor gun is an English piece of equipment, it has two barrels on it, and we could fire in case we saw a submarine, we could fire it with depth charges. And I -- they assigned me to a -- an English youngster, he was in his late teens, and he used to like to come to Boston Harbor, he used to like to cuss American all the time, used to cuss. He said, "Mate, I've got to tell you something," and by the way, the temperatures in the Atlantic were very -- were very cold, you know, I mean you couldn't last very long. He said, "I want to tell you something that you should know." I said, "What's that?" He said, "You know, if we ever get bombed, you hit the water, you got three minutes to live." I never forgot that. Here I'm on this ship and the wind's blowing like heck and I'm at the Bofor gun and I'm listening to this Limey kid, and he said -- because I call the British Limey, by the way, and I called him -- oh, yeah, we had a Canadian soldier, I called him -- in the front lines outside of Normandy, I called him Kanooks. I called the Canadians Kanooks, and I called the British Limeys -- well, Limeys. I didn't mean to be derogatory. I was being complimentary, too, because they were with us, and we went through many battles together. And -- and I want to thank the States, my -- my mother and my relatives always said prayers for us, and the good Lord willing, the good Lord listened, I thank God I made it, and I want to thank God for one thing. Out of five, I didn't get any what they call Purple Hearts. I could have gotten a few, but I didn't accept them. I cut my hand on a K-ration or I hit something and I could have went to the medics and picked up a Purple Heart, whatever, but I mean, the ones that deserve it deserve it, don't get me wrong, they got injured or killed there, they deserve Purple Hearts, that I respect. And I believe in this country. It's the greatest country in the world. But duty, honor, country, that's -- I can say that as long as I live, and I -- by the way, I have on me an Army band, I picked it up at Beatty's, downtown Cleveland, 1942. And on this Army band, it's platinum, it's got my name, serial number, that's all it had on it, my name and serial number, but then on the back of it, what I did is I -- when I got through, I went back to Beatty's and they inserted ETO, it means European Theater of Operations, and my serial number, 15307859. A one means I enlisted. I was proud of that. 15307859, a -- beyond it it has five battle stars. That's all I put on there, and I still have it to this day, since 1942. But those are the memories we take with us, and I -- I regret that some of the situations that happened recently, I went to the funeral of First Sergeant Dowdy at Slavik Village on Fleet Avenue, and I reminisced thinking about him, who was killed in action. Here was a man that -- a soldier that had 20 years, one more year, he would have been retired, and here he got into Iraq and got into this combat situation and he was killed, and I never forgot the services there, because I was honored as a Veteran of Foreign War Honor Guard for Sergeant -- First Sergeant Dowdy here in Cleveland. So, militarily, I don't know, it just seems to go on and on, and we should never -- never fail to -- never fail to recognize the Serviceman, what he goes through, and I lost many good friends in World War II and -- where else? I had some friends of mine that were with the Marine Corps. We lost a friend of mine who was a schoolmate at West Tech called Stanley Bokevich (ph). He -- he was on Iwo Jima, and Stanley received a Silver Star, two Purple Hearts and was supposed to get the Congressional Medal of Honor for Iwo Jima, because he hit the beach twice, and on the second time that he hit the beach, he was hit by a sniper, he never made it. And Henry Kaballa (ph), another Marine, hit Okinawa, and I had a friend of mine called Stanley -- Staff Sergeant Stanley Godak (ph), who survived the Bataanic Rigor Death March with General MacArthur, and Stanley Godak came back, and he only weighed 90 pounds, but he said I buried many Americans on the Death March, which the Japanese made us do. He says, "They never gave us food or anything, they kept on hitting our thighs with clubs," and he survived, and he said, "I'll never regret the trouble I went through, but the people I left behind, I regret." That's the same thing with me. I -- I've been asked to go to Normandy in honor of the crosses that are there, and I haven't been able to for several personal reasons, but Normandy I would like to go to. I would like to go to a town called Hamm, Luxembourg. Hamm, Luxembourg is a small town outside of Bastogne, and buried there are American Servicemen from the Battle of the Bulge. Ironically, with them is the commander, General George F. Patton, Junior. He's buried with his men in Hamm, H A M M, Luxembourg. That I would like to have gone back to to pay respects to, and those are the memories I carry with me today. But I -- I wish that we could somehow -- MacArthur said it all. He'd give all his victory, all his battle gear -- mentions about the military recognition for one thing, if we could stop wars, if we could -- humanity-wise could discuss these things without going into combat, because that leads into more difficulties as time goes by. But the one thing you got to remember about combat and the military situation that people seem to forget in their own way, the people, I told you about that 417,000 World War II and the 56,000 Korea, 58,000 in Vietnam and the others that are killed in combat, the one thing you've got to remember, which I think people forget, are the families that suffer this as life goes on. They cannot forget, they do not forget, because these people, the parents, parents, maybe wives and husbands, sometimes women got killed, too, and parents and children never forget combat, because what they did, they did for their country, but these people should be remembered, too, the ones that are suffering while they live to what they went through. I am speaking for all American Servicemen. I believe in that heritage of duty, honor, country.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That covers it?

sp.speaker: Theodore E. Sliwa
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Thank you. [Tape recorder turned off, then restarted for additional discussion.]

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: All right, tell me about Bob Hope.

sp.speaker: Theodore E. Sliwa
sp.p: Well, I -- after the war, on the 18th of August of 1945 in a town called Friedberg, Germany, I went to a USO show, and ironically, I ran into a comedian, which was famous at the time and at this time today, is Bob Hope, and he signed my -- an autograph -- I says, "By the way, I want you to sign something for me in remembrance of today." He says, "Okay." He put down, "Remember Cleveland, Euclid Beach, Bob Hope," and he signed it on August the 18th, 1945, Friedberg, Germany.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So, did you go to a show then?

sp.speaker: Theodore E. Sliwa
sp.p: Yes, I did. He had a very good show, and we were very pleased. One thing I must say about USO at times -- I even saw Bing Crosby, too, by the way. Morally, people that were in the Service, when they get somebody like that from the States from the USO, it sort of brings them back -- fond memories in remembrance of their own -- where they came from, and it really was a very good thing. It's commendable. The USO has been very commendable. And I must say one more thing, at times we came across the Red Cross from time to time, and they gave you coffee and doughnuts, but I didn't see too many, because being on the front lines quite a bit. I ran into them as I was coming home, I ran into the Red Cross, and they'd give us coffee and doughnuts at the train stations. That I appreciated also. That's a good moral feeling for all Servicemen.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Very good. Anything else we're forgetting?

sp.speaker: Theodore E. Sliwa
sp.p: No, I -- I --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I'm glad we remembered that.

sp.speaker: Theodore E. Sliwa
sp.p: Let's see, I would like to also comment that the letters that we received from people from home morally did help. We used to have a thing called mail call, and by God, those were very important to us from time to time when we'd see mail call, but once in a while we'd receive packages, and in them had fruitcakes and whatever could keep in being transported and certain items in there that we really appreciated from the States. I mean, the food they would send us, cookies and candy, were very much appreciated. So, don't -- if you ever send anybody anything overseas, military men, be sure to remember them by sending them something -- packages of food. They appreciate that very much, and basically letters. Those are -- morally, they're very helpful, and psychologically, so I encourage that very much.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: All right, okay.

sp.speaker: Theodore E. Sliwa
sp.p: Looking back, I fondly remember two more things that I should comment about, and that's that Cary Grant, who was one of our famous actors, he was one of the finest men. He came from England at the age of 16, but he came to really be a good American, and he became a good American. In fact, in the war days, he enlisted in the Service, but they told him not to, because they could use him for -- for various shows and also for selling war bonds, which he did very commendably. And I would like to comment one thing about James Stewart, who to me epitomizes one of the finest American actors you can find, and humble as he is and the way he talks, what a great American Irishman, but anyway, James Stewart, he got in the Service, by the way, as a private, and he -- and he got in the Air Corps and worked himself up through the ranks, and somehow he became an officer, and during World War II, he became a lieutenant in the Air Corps, and he was a -- on something like 15 air raids in England as a commander of the ships, but you never knew it about him. He never talked much about his military background, but commendably, he was very well respected by his men, and he served admirably as a commander of a bomber over England, and I think he should be remembered and not forgotten. People like that gave all for their country. I mean, they were actors and actresses, but basically they were American. That I never will forget.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That's it?

sp.speaker: Theodore E. Sliwa
sp.p: That's it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Okay.
[Interview concluded.]
